meaning: Each tie names the phrase of the paper that a Lean declaration states, as read side by side for Proof Reader (wcook04/proof-reader 3858afbe00b2, papers/navier-stokes-paper). Titles, reading notes, topics and comparisons are AI-drafted or AI-assessed; no mathematician has reviewed them. Surviving exact quotes in marked paragraphs retain their existing links. Revised explanations link to declarations in the pinned Lean source.

families.name: From a certificate to a profile
From cell data to the certificate

topics.name: The blow-up statements
topics.description: Smooth solutions, breakdown on space and on the torus, and the theorems that state them (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1).

topics.name: The fractional extension
topics.description: The authors' separate extension with dissipation exponent between 1 and 5/4, outside the classical paper.

topics.name: Heat flow and mild solutions
topics.description: The heat semigroup, the bilinear Duhamel term, mild solutions, restarting and uniqueness (§3).

topics.name: Recurrent profiles
topics.description: Self-similar time-periodic profiles, their slices and orbits, and weak profiles read as physical fields (§2, §4.1, §7.11).

topics.name: Monodromy and the correction
topics.description: The period map, its compact-plus-small splitting, the spectral projection and the fixed point that corrects a profile to an exact solution (§4).

topics.name: Passing to the torus
topics.description: The solenoidal cutoff, periodization and the periodic right inverse that move the construction onto the torus (§5–6).

topics.name: From certificate to profile
topics.description: Certificate data, the free operator, convection, held solutions and the smoothing of the weak profile they produce (§7).

topics.name: The coercive multiplier estimate
topics.description: The multiplier, its five density coefficients and lower bound, and the a priori estimate it gives (Appendix B.1 and B.2).

topics.name: Encoded cell data
topics.description: The finitely represented inputs: coordinates and harmonics, the profile representation, splines and jets, physical cells, rows, weights and potentials.

topics.name: Reduction to the quarter plane
topics.description: Symmetry reduction of the density to the meridian quarter plane (B.3).

topics.name: Cells, traces and tails
topics.description: Integrability, the common vector of unknowns, resolved modes, the tail budget and the exterior estimate (B.4).

topics.name: Angular and ray-exterior tests
topics.description: The angular inequalities, the pointwise test and the integrated test on ray exteriors (B.5 and B.6).

topics.name: The matrix tree lower bound
topics.description: The tree conditions on the cell matrices and the passage from all cells to the global inequality (B.7 and B.8).

topics.name: Changing the profile
topics.description: Bounds for moving estimates from the reference field to the actual profile (B.9).

topics.name: The adjoint pairing and its error
topics.description: The quadratic adjoint pairing, the azimuthal dual norm and the linear adjoint error with potentials and pins (B.10 to B.12).

topics.name: The offset and the certificate
topics.description: Enclosing the constant, linear and quadratic offset, and the fifteen fields of CellSystemCondition that make the data a certificate (B.13 and B.14).

notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou:
Fix any index j among the k certificate indices, a real field ψ(θ,y), center fields Wα⁰, fitted direction fields Wⁱ for i in a finite set I, and remaining fields Zαⁱ for i outside I; all fields are defined for real θ and y∈ℝ³. Membership j∈𝒥 is not required by this condition, although Lemma B.12 uses it for indices in 𝒥. The parameter set is 𝒦={α:|αi|≤ρi for i∈𝒥, ∑_{i∉𝒥}(diαi)²≤ρ*²}. The proposed coordinate bounds ρ̄i must satisfy ρi≤ρ̄i on 𝒥 and, off 𝒥, di≠0 and |ρ*|≤|di|ρ̄i.

For the center and each fitted direction s∈{0}∪I, supply potentials Gs,Us,Fs,qs and four nonnegative numbers nG,s,nU,s,nF,s,nR,s. Over [0,1]×ℝ³, require ‖Gs‖₂≤nG,s, ‖∇Us‖₂≤nU,s and ‖Fs‖₂≤nF,s, with Frobenius norms for matrices. Here this norm notation denotes bounds on the nonnegative extended integrals of the squares. The condition does not itself require measurability of these potential fields; that is needed for their usual L² interpretation. Put K=∇ψ−∑lYl[∇Φ̃l−(∇Φ̃l)ᵀ]. At the center, for every α∈𝒦, the residual Tα⁰−div K+∇q₀+∆G₀+w*∆U₀−div F₀ must have dual bound nR,0, where Tα⁰=−S₀⁻¹∂θψ−ψ−(y·∇)ψ/2+(DWα⁰)ᵀψ−(Wα⁰·∇)ψ. For each i∈I, the residual Ti+∇qi+∆Gi+w*∆Ui−div Fi must have dual bound nR,i, where Ti=(DWⁱ)ᵀψ−(Wⁱ·∇)ψ−ςi∂θψ. Matrix divergence means ∑a∂a(F ea), so the paper writes the flux divergence with a transpose under its matrix convention.

Here a dual bound n means a pointwise decomposition into two measurable summands with nonnegative allowances whose sum is at most n. One summand obeys 2‖|y|R′‖₂≤n′. Each of the three complex components R″₁+iR″₂, R″₁−iR″₂, R″₃ of the other is, at every time and almost everywhere in space, a finite sum e^{2πik′θ}g(y), with distinct integer frequency pairs per component and g(Rφy)=e^{ikφ}g(y). The sum of (|k|+1/2)⁻²∫|y|²|g|², counting each transverse component with weight 1/2, is at most n″². This is the condition before Lemma B.11 with the paper's separate periodicity requirement omitted.

For every i∉I require ϖi>0, and require nv,nd≥0. Uniformly for α∈𝒦, require ∫₀¹∫ℝ³(∑_{i∉I}ϖi|Zαⁱ|²)|ψ|²≤nv². There must be common bounds δi such that each (DZαⁱ)ᵀψ has dual bound δi for every α and ∑_{i∉I}ϖiδi²≤nd². The field ∂θψ must have dual bound nθ.

For the potential fields Φl, their replacements Φ̃l and the matrix-valued constraint fields Ξl, require nΦ,cΞ≥0, ‖∑lYl(Φl−Φ̃l)‖₂≤nΦ, and ‖∑lcl(Ξl−∇Φl)‖₂²≤cΞ²∑lcl² for every real vector c. Also require the Euclidean coefficient bound |Y|≤nY. Field norms and integrals are over [0,1]×ℝ³; the coefficient norms are finite-dimensional Euclidean norms.

Define Ds=[nG,s²+(w*nU,s+nF,s+nR,s)²/w*]¹ᐟ². The required total inequality is D₀+∑_{i∈I}ρ̄iDi+{[∑_{i∉I}ρ̄i²/ϖi]¹ᐟ²(nv+nd)+(∑_{i∉I}|ςi|ρ̄i)nθ}/√w*+nΦ+nYcΞ/√w*≤aj. This is the explicit generalization of (B.53) with selected directions treated by their own potentials; I empty gives the paper's collective treatment. The condition alone does not identify these supplied fields with the profile and adjoint of a certificate or impose their regularity, periodicity or w*>0. Those are separate linking and representation hypotheses. Division by zero and the square root of a negative number are defined to be zero in the raw formulas, so positive w* is needed for the stated energy interpretation.

This field of the adjoint-defect assumptions requires, for every real coefficient vector x∈ℝⁿ, ∫₀¹∫_{ℝ³}|∑ᵢx_i(Ξ_i−∇Φ_i)|_F²≤c_Ξ²∑ᵢx_i². The matrix square is the sum of squared Euclidean norms of its columns, so the left side is the squared H norm in the paper. The integral is initially nonnegative and may be infinite; the finite right side bounds it. Nonnegativity of c_Ξ is required elsewhere in the same data condition. Consequently this squared inequality gives ‖∑ᵢx_i(Ξ_i−∇Φ_i)‖_H≤c_Ξ|x|. The hypothesis concerns all x, including combinations of distinct constraints; it is stronger than independent bounds for the individual tensors.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt: Let $w_*>0$. For potential bounds $n=(n_G,n_U,n_F,n_R)$ put $D(n)=\sqrt{n_G^2+(w_*n_U+n_F+n_R)^2/w_*}$. If a finite set $I$ of parameter directions has its own fitted potential bounds $n^{(i)}$, this definition is $D(n^{(0)})+\sum_{i\in I}\bar\varrho_iD(n^{(i)})+w_*^{-1/2}\{[\sum_{i\notin I}\bar\varrho_i^2/\varpi_i]^{1/2}(n_{\mathrm v}+n_{\mathrm d})+[\sum_{i\notin I}|\varsigma_i|\bar\varrho_i]n_\theta\}$. The paper-specific identification sets $I=\varnothing$, leaving the first two terms of (B.53). The constraint replacement charge is added separately. The definition itself accepts arbitrary real inputs and takes division by zero to be zero and the square root of a negative real number to be zero; its application requires $w_*>0$ and $\varpi_i>0$, and nonnegative norm bounds. It is a proposed numerical budget, with no assertion here that the fields satisfy it.

This definition forms $n_\Phi+n_Yc_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*}$. Here $n_\Phi$ bounds $\|\sum_lY_{jl}(\Phi_l-\widetilde\Phi_l)\|_{\mathcal H}$, $n_Y$ bounds the Euclidean norm of the row $(Y_{jl})_l$, and $c_\Xi$ controls the $L^2$ matrix error in replacing $\Xi_l$ by $\nabla\Phi_l$. The two contributions pair with $\Delta v$ and $\nabla v$ respectively. For a positive constant weight they give the last part of (B.53) after division by the energy norm. This declaration defines the number; the assertions that it bounds those pairings, and that the indicated numbers bound the norms, are separate statements. Division by zero is defined to be zero, but the intended use has $w_*=39/50>0$.

For the fixed adjoint $\psi_j$, compact generators $\widetilde\Phi_l$ and real coefficients $Y_{jl}$, this definition forms $K=
abla\psi_j-\sum_lY_{jl}(
abla\widetilde\Phi_l-(
abla\widetilde\Phi_l)^{\mathsf T})$. A gradient is represented by the map that sends a coordinate vector to the corresponding directional derivative. Thus the divergence of this matrix map is $\Delta\psi_j-\sum_lY_{jl}(\Delta\widetilde\Phi_l-
abla\operatorname{div}\widetilde\Phi_l)$. For the divergence-free generators of the paper, $-\operatorname{div}K=-\Delta\psi_j+\sum_lY_{jl}\Delta\widetilde\Phi_l$, which supplies precisely those terms in (B.52). The definition alone does not assert regularity or divergence-freeness. The skew part of the generator gradient is retained explicitly in the general formal construction. In this definition a pointwise derivative is zero wherever the corresponding function is not differentiable. Regularity is needed before these expressions can be read as distributional derivatives.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded: Let $R$ be a measurable real vector field on $\mathbb R_\theta\times\mathbb R_y^3$, and let $n\ge0$. The condition represents each of $R_1+iR_2$, $R_1-iR_2$ and $R_3$, almost everywhere in $y$ for every $\theta$, as a finite sum $\sum e^{2\pi i k'\theta}g(y)$. Each amplitude is measurable and satisfies $g(R_\phi y)=e^{ik\phi}g(y)$ for every angle and point. The integers $k',k$ are distinct as pairs within each component. It requires $\sum c\,(|k|+1/2)^{-2}\int|y|^2|g|^2\le n^2$, with $c=1/2$ for each horizontal complex component and $c=1$ for the third. The denominator is positive for every integer $k$, including zero. The representation implies period one almost everywhere; exact pointwise periodicity is not a separate assumption. These are the harmonic terms called $R''$ in the paper's dual bound.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.I: For real vectors $v,R\in\mathbb R^3$, define $v^+=v_1+iv_2$, $v^-=v_1-iv_2$ and $v^0=v_3$, and use the same convention for $R$. The formal statement proves $v\cdot R=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{v^+}R^+)+\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{v^-}R^-)+v_3R_3$. This is an identity of real numbers, with no regularity or integrability hypotheses. It is the component decomposition used at the end of the proof of Lemma B.11. The two horizontal factors are $1/2$; the vertical factor is $1$. The formal component labels begin at zero and refer in order to $+$, $-$ and the vertical component.

For any real matrix $M:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, let $M^+$, $M^-$ and $M^0$ be the matrices obtained by taking the two horizontal rows as a complex pair, its conjugate, and the vertical row. The formal statement proves $\tfrac12|M^+|^2+\tfrac12|M^-|^2+|M^0|^2=|M|^2$, where each squared norm is the sum of the squared absolute values of its entries, and the complex pair is represented by its two real coordinates. Taking $M=\nabla v$ gives the weighted gradient identity in the proof of Lemma B.11. The formal theorem is purely algebraic for every matrix; applying it almost everywhere and integrating gives the same identity for any weakly differentiable field with finite gradient energy. No symmetry, periodicity or solenoidality is assumed.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.g: For a measurable matrix field $G:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, the formal statement proves that the sum over all integer azimuthal modes of its gradient energy in the rotating cylindrical frame is at most $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|G|^2$. The mode energy is integrated with cylindrical measure $2\pi r\,dr\,dz$ on $r>0$, $z\in\mathbb R$; the matrix norm on the right is the sum of squares of all entries. Both sides are nonnegative extended integrals. The statement applies to any measurable matrix field, without requiring that it be the derivative of a velocity. This is the spatial Fourier-energy estimate used to pass from single-mode inequalities to the total bound. Projection in the time variable is a separate operation.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m: Let $v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and its weak gradient $G$ be measurable, with $v\in L^6$ and $G\in L^2$. Put $U=v_1+iv_2$, and let $U_k(r,z)$ be its normalized angular Fourier coefficient. Given the smooth azimuthal estimate, approximation by smooth compactly supported fields in gradient norm and local $L^2$, and the bound of the total Fourier gradient energy by $\int|G|^2$, the formal statement proves $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(|k|+1/2)^2\,2\pi\int_{r>0,z\in\mathbb R}r|U_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)\,dr\,dz\le\int|G|^2$. Thus it controls all angular projections together. The paper states (B.50) for a single complex field already having wave number $k$; representing that field by two real components yields its special case. The three analytic premises are supplied by separate proved declarations in the formalisation. No divergence or reflection assumption on $v$ occurs.

Let $u,B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C$ be measurable, and assume $B(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi,z)=e^{ik\phi}B(r,0,z)$ for an integer $k$. Let $u_k(r,z)$ be the angular coefficient normalized by $1/(2\pi)$. The formal statement gives $|\int\overline{u}B|^2\le[2\pi\int_{r>0,z\in\mathbb R}r|u_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)]\,[\int|y|^2|B|^2]$. This uses Cauchy–Schwarz after angular projection; combining it with the azimuthal Hardy estimate produces the factor $(|k|+1/2)^{-1}$ in the paper. The displayed conclusion uses the opposite complex conjugation from the paper's pairing, which has the same absolute value. There is no hypothesis that the ordinary complex integral on the left exists in the analytic sense. If its integrand is not integrable, that integral is assigned the value zero. The right-hand side uses nonnegative integrals, which may equal infinity. Thus this statement alone does not establish integrability of the pairing. In the application, finite weighted bounds and a separate integrability theorem justify its ordinary analytic interpretation.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.s: Let $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth with compact support, and let $U=u_1+iu_2$. For any integer $k$, form the angular coefficient $U_k(r,z)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{-ik\phi}U(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi,z)\,d\phi$. The formal statement bounds $(|k|+1/2)^2\,2\pi\int_{r>0}\int_{\mathbb R}r|U_k(r,z)|^2/(r^2+z^2)\,dz\,dr$ by the corresponding Fourier component of the full gradient energy, represented in the rotating cylindrical frame. It is a statement about an angular projection of a smooth real vector field. Taking $u=(\operatorname{Re}U,\operatorname{Im}U,0)$ when $U$ already has wave number $k$ gives the smooth scalar inequality in (B.50). Extending to an $L^6$ field with a weak $L^2$ gradient requires the separate approximation result. The denominator is nonzero on $r>0$.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.t: Take a finite family of measurable complex amplitudes $a_p(y)$ and distinct integer temporal frequencies $k'_p$. The formal statement proves $\int_0^1\int|y|^2|\sum_p e^{2\pi i k'_p\theta}a_p(y)|^2\,dy\,d\theta\le\sum_p\int|y|^2|a_p(y)|^2\,dy$. Both sides are nonnegative extended integrals. The frequencies need be distinct only on the selected finite index set. For every real θ and every closed spatial ball, assume that p(θ,·) is Lipschitz on that ball, with a constant that may depend on θ and on the ball. The formal statement concludes that the spatial gradient is measurable and that its ordinary integral against every smooth, compactly supported space-time test field φ with div_y φ=0 has value zero: ∫_{ℝ×ℝ³}∇_yp·φ=0. The spatial derivative is defined everywhere, with value zero where differentiability fails; on each time slice it agrees almost everywhere with the weak spatial gradient. Mesh, joins and vanishing coefficient conditions are separate; this definition alone asserts no compact support, L² bound or divergence freedom of Φ.
notes.Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement:
Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space with the heat and bilinear operators of §3.4: $G(t)$ is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, $K(\tau)$ is symmetric, continuous for $\tau>0$, obeys $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Suppose the dilations satisfy $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for positive scales, with continuous dependence on scale. Assume $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for a dense set of $f$ and every $\tau>0$.

Let $S>0$, let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G$, $K$ and $D$, and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ and the similarity-time mild equation. Here that equation uses $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\mathcal K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$ and reads $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-s_0)w(s_0)+\int_{s_0}^{s}\mathcal K(s-r)(w(r),w(r))\,dr$ for $s_0\le s$.

Fix a positive natural number $k$, put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$ and $L=1-\mu$, and define $u_n(\sigma)=D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$ for $0\le\sigma\le L$. For every natural $n$, the formal statement asserts that $u_n$ is a continuous mild solution, $D_\mu u_n(L)=u_{n+1}(0)$, $u_{n+k}(\sigma)=\rho u_n(\sigma)$, and $\|u_n\|_{C([0,L];X)}\le e^{S/(4k)}M$ whenever $\|w(s)\|\le M$ for all real $s$. Thus the period is split into $k$ pieces. It gives no positive lower bound on $\|u^*(t)\|$. Curves on the compact interval are extended constantly beyond either endpoint when an everywhere-defined function is needed; the mildness assertion concerns only the interval. Positivity of $k$ prevents division by zero in $S/k$.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.
notes.Breakdown.RestrictStatement: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. The assertion is the following implication. Let $a\le m\le t$, and let $u:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ be continuous on $[a,t]$. Suppose the quadratic Duhamel integrals are Bochner integrable and the identities $u(r)=G(r-a)u(a)+\int_a^rK(r-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ hold at $r=m$ and $r=t$. Then the integral from $m$ to $t$ is Bochner integrable and $u(t)=G(t-m)u(m)+\int_m^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. The endpoints may coincide. Only the two indicated initial-time identities are needed. Formula (3.13) allows independent continuous factors $f,h$ in the integrand; this formal statement treats the quadratic case $f=h=u$.
notes.Breakdown.SectionInternal.exists_preimag: Let $X$ be a real normed space, let $P:X\to X$ be bounded and linear with finite-dimensional range, and let $C\subset X$ be a dense linear subspace. For every $v\in\operatorname{ran}P$, the formal statement proves the existence of $c\in C$ with $Pc=v$. Neither completeness of $X$ nor the projection identity $P^2=P$ is required. Taking preimages of the vectors of a basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$ is the finite-dimensional step used to choose the compactly supported correction space in Proposition 4.3. The statement concerns individual preimages; their linear organization and boundedness are supplied by the subsequent lifting construction.
notes.Breakdown.SectionStatement: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space, $P:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ a bounded linear projection with finite-dimensional range, and $C'\subset\mathcal X$ a dense real linear subspace. The assertion is that there is a bounded linear map $J:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ with $PJ=P$ and $Jx\in C'$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$. Thus a prescribed component in the range of $P$ can be represented by a datum in $C'$. In the application $C'$ consists of smooth compactly supported divergence-free fields, and $J(\operatorname{range}P)$ is finite-dimensional because the domain of this restriction is finite-dimensional. The statement does not say that the full image of $J$ is finite-dimensional, nor does it prescribe a bound on $\|J\|$ or require eigenfunctions to be smooth or compactly supported.
notes.Breakdown.SimilarityResidual:
For functions $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$, the value at $(s,y)$ is $\partial_sW+ rac12W+ rac12(y\cdot

Nor does the definition itself assume differentiability: derivative operations have assigned values where a classical derivative does not exist. In every smooth-profile application the smoothness hypotheses ensure that all terms are the ordinary derivatives appearing in (1.2). The spatial Laplacian is the sum of the pure second derivatives, and the spatial derivative of $W$ applied to $y$ is $(y\cdot

notes.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.IsHsCurve: For a nonnegative integer $m$, a Fourier field $F(t,\xi)\in\mathbb C^3$ and real $a,b$, the condition asserts measurability of $F(t,\cdot)$ and finiteness of $\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\xi|^2)^m|F(t,\xi)|^2\,d\xi$ for each $t\in[a,b]$. It also requires that this same integral for $F(t,\cdot)-F(t_0,\cdot)$ tend to zero as $t\to t_0$ within $[a,b]$. Thus it expresses strong continuity in $H^m$, with Fourier normalization $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$ and an equivalent Sobolev weight omitting the powers of $2\pi$. The order $m$ is an integer. This definition alone contains neither the Navier–Stokes equation nor an $L^2_tH^{m+1}_x$ bound.
notes.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.exists_symbolFlow_o: Let $T>0$ and let $F_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^3$ be measurable, conjugate symmetric and pointwise orthogonal to $\xi$, with $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^3|F_0|^2<\infty$. Suppose the bound $\int|\xi|^2|F(t,\xi)|^2\,d\xi\leq M_+$, where $M_+=\max(M,0)$ for a supplied real $M$, holds for every $H^3$-continuous solenoidal Fourier solution $F$ of the unforced integral equation with initial value $F_0$ on every partial interval $[0,s]\subset[0,T]$, at all $t\leq s$. Then such a solution exists on $[0,T]$. Its velocity gradient has squared norm $4\pi^2\int|\xi|^2|F|^2$. The hypothesis quantifies over all partial solutions and assumes $H^3$ initial data; the conclusion is continuation, without the alternative of a maximal $H^1$ solution with diverging norm stated in Tao’s corollary.
notes.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.isHsCurve_of_flow: Let $F(t,\xi)$ be a Fourier solution of the unforced Navier–Stokes integral equation on $[0,s]$, continuous in the norm $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^3|F|^2$. Assume $\xi\cdot F(t,\xi)=0$ and $F(t,-\xi)=\overline{F(t,\xi)}$ at every time and frequency, and $F(0)=F_0$. If $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^m|F_0|^2<\infty$ for every nonnegative integer $m$, then $t\mapsto F(t)$ is continuous in every one of these Sobolev norms on $[0,s]$. The heat multiplier is $e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}$. This statement concerns spatial Sobolev regularity; smoothness in time and the construction of the pressure are separate results.
notes.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.isSolutionOn_physFi: Let $T>0$ and let $F(t,\xi)$ solve the unforced projected Fourier integral equation on $[0,T]$. Assume strong continuity in every norm $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^m|F|^2$, for nonnegative integers $m$, and pointwise solenoidality and conjugate symmetry. Let $U$ be the real inverse Fourier transform of $F$, and let $P$ be the real inverse Fourier transform of $-\xi\cdot\widehat{(U\cdot\nabla)U}/(2\pi i|\xi|^2)$. The formal statement gives smoothness of both fields on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, incompressibility on the closed interval, and the viscosity-one momentum equation for $0<t<T$. Division by zero assigns the pressure coefficient at $\xi=0$ the value zero; changing one frequency does not change the inverse Fourier integral. The hypotheses contain all spatial Sobolev orders and the integral equation, rather than smooth initial data alone.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.Complexification.isCo:
Let $X$ be a real inner-product space and $T:X\to X$ a bounded compact real-linear operator.

The formal statement proves that $T_{\mathbb C}(x+iy)=Tx+iTy$ is compact on the complexification, whose norm satisfies $\|x+iy\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$. The conclusion justifies carrying the compact difference between the monodromy and the free operator into the complex setting. It is separate from the equality of their real and complex operator norms and from every assertion about the essential spectrum.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.Complexification.norm:
Let $X$ be a real inner-product space and $T:X\to X$ a bounded real-linear operator. Its complexification acts on pairs written $x+iy$ by $T_{\mathbb C}(x+iy)=Tx+iTy$, with norm $\|x+iy\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$.

The formal statement proves $\|T_{\mathbb C}\|\le\|T\|$. The paper says that the two norms are equal. The reverse inequality follows by restricting to the isometric copy $x\mapsto x+i0$, but is not the conclusion of this formal statement. No compactness or spectral assumption is involved.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.exists_annulus:
Let $Y$ be a complex Banach space, let $T_0,C$ be bounded linear operators with $C$ compact and $\|T_0\|\le b\le\alpha<\beta$.

The formal statement proves that there exist $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$ such that every complex $z$ with $r_1\le|z|\le r_2$ lies in the resolvent set of $T_0+C$. Thus it gives a whole closed annulus without spectrum, which is stronger than selecting only one circle $|z|=\Theta$. In the application $\alpha=e^{-S/4}$ and $\beta=1$, any intermediate circle in this annulus can be used for the splitting. No particular numerical values for the radii are supplied.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.finite_spectrum_outsi:
Let $Y$ be a complex Banach space, $T_0,C:Y\to Y$ bounded linear operators, and suppose $C$ is compact and $\|T_0\|\le b<r$.

The formal statement proves that $\{z\in\sigma(T_0+C):|z|\ge r\}$ is finite. Since an operator norm is nonnegative, the hypotheses imply $r>0$. The spectrum is the set where $zI-(T_0+C)$ fails to have a bounded inverse. This is the finiteness conclusion used to select a circle avoiding the spectrum in Lemma 4.5. The formal statement does not state equality of essential spectral radii, poles of the resolvent, or their algebraic multiplicities; those are the paper’s cited route to the same finiteness conclusion.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.norm_backProj_le:
Let $T$ be a bounded operator on a complex Banach space, and let $0<r<R$ with $\|T\|<R$ and $|z|=r$ contained in the resolvent set. Define $B_n=(2\pi i)^{-1}(\int_{|z|=R}z^{-n}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz-\int_{|z|=r}z^{-n}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz)$.

The formal statement proves that some $K>0$ satisfies $\|B_n\|\le Kr^{-n}$ for every natural $n$. A separate contour identity gives $T^nB_n=I-Q$, where $Q$ is the interior projection; this identifies the exterior inverse powers. Choosing $r>\Theta$ yields summability after multiplication by $\Theta^n$. Both contours have positive radius, so the powers $z^{-n}$ never divide by zero on them.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.norm_pow_mul_specProj:
Let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on a complex Banach space, and let $r>0$ with every point of $|z|=r$ in the resolvent set. Put $Q=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{|z|=r}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz$.

The formal statement proves the existence of $K>0$ such that $\|T^nQ\|\le Kr^n$ for every natural $n\ge0$. This is a contour-integral power estimate, stated at the contour radius. To obtain the first series of (4.11), use a radius $r<\Theta$ in the spectrum-free annulus and the equality of projections for those circles, then sum $K(r/\Theta)^n$. It gives the needed geometric bound without identifying the constant with the paper’s implicit constant.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.specProj: For a bounded operator $T$ on a complex normed space and real radius $r$, this defines $Q=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{|z|=r}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz$, with the circle traversed counterclockwise. If the space is complete, $r>0$ and the circle lies in the resolvent set, this is the spectral projection for the spectrum inside the circle. The paper denotes the projection for the exterior spectrum by $P$; with its $\Theta=r$, the corresponding operator is $P=I-Q$. The definition alone requires neither a spectral gap nor idempotence, and its total resolvent takes the value zero when an inverse does not exist. The spectral theorems impose the resolvent-set hypothesis before interpreting the integral as a projection. The contour integral is a parametrized Bochner integral; if it is not integrable, the integral is assigned zero. Completeness and the resolvent-set hypothesis provide the ordinary spectral interpretation.
notes.Breakdown.StepDataStatement:
Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $\rho$ be a linear isometry of $X$ onto itself commuting with $G,K,D$ for all their real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ with $S>0$. Put $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

For every dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the assertion supplies an integer $k\ge1$ and a real $\theta$ with $\delta=1-e^{-S/k}\le t_0$ and $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $Y=C([0,\delta];X)$ with its supremum norm, $u_n^*(\tau)=D_{(1-\tau)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\tau))$, $B_\delta(f,g)(\tau)=\int_0^\tau K(\tau-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$, $A_n=2B_\delta(u_n^*,\cdot)$, $\Gamma x(\tau)=G(\tau)x$, and $Lv=D_\mu v(\delta)$. It asserts $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for all nonnegative integers $n$, and supplies a finite dimensional subspace $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C'$, and a bounded linear map $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)$. If $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, then $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. This is a statement of the linear correction on successive intervals; the correction of the datum is $Je\in C'$. The smooth compactly supported space $E$ of the paper is represented by $J(V)$ when $C'$ is the corresponding dense data space. The formula uses only positive $k$, $\mu$, $\theta$ and $1-\tau$, so their reciprocals are ordinary ones. The path operators are formally assigned zero if their required continuous realizations do not exist; the analytic construction for $\delta>0$ proves those realizations before using them.

The product norm controlled by $\mathcal R$ is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. A bound for the actual datum correction $Je$ also uses $\|J\|$. The assertion concerns sequences of compact-interval paths, whereas Proposition 4.3 is phrased for a global weighted curve.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.
notes.Breakdown.Symmetry: A symmetry is a pair $(R,\theta_0)$, where $R$ is an invertible real linear isometry of Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ and $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$. Thus $R\in O(3)$; orientation reversal is allowed. A collection $\Gamma$ is an arbitrary set of such pairs and may be empty. Neither closure under composition nor a group structure is required. Invariance of a field under a pair is a separate condition.
notes.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The transfer chooses data in any given dense space and provides a positive-power error bound after restoring similarity scale. Smoothness, finite kinetic energy, the full corrected-data family and all quantitative clauses of Theorem 1.1 require further results.
notes.Breakdown.UniqueStatement: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. This assertion says that two mild solutions $u,v:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ with $u(a)=v(a)$ coincide throughout $[a,b)$ if both are continuous and satisfy the quadratic Duhamel equation there, and throughout $[a,b]$ if both satisfy the closed-interval version. Each Duhamel integral is required to be Bochner integrable. The initial and final times are finite real numbers. Equality is asserted only on the indicated interval; arbitrary values assigned outside it are unrestricted. There is no smallness assumption on the common datum or on the length of the interval. The closed-interval conclusion is the uniqueness clause of Lemma 3.5, and the half-open conclusion is also included.
notes.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.conti: The formal kernel argument uses continuity in positive time and bilinear estimates for the varying arguments.
notes.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.norm_: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Assume that $G(t)$, $t\geq0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, and that $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear map on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $\|K(\tau)\|\leq C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\leq1$ and $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\geq0$, $\tau>0$. Let $a\leq b$ and let $u,v:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ satisfy $\|u(s)\|\leq M$ and $\|v(s)\|\leq N$ on $[a,b]$. Extend their restrictions by the endpoint values outside this interval. For any $t\in\mathbb R$ and $0<r\leq1$, the formal statement gives $\|K(r)(u(c(t-r)),v(c(t-r)))\|\leq C_KMN r^{-3/4}$, where $c(s)=\max(a,\min(b,s))$. For $a\leq t-r\leq b$ the endpoint extension disappears. This particular estimate has the additional restriction $r\leq1$.
notes.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralStatement: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. This is the assertion that, if $a\le b$, $u,v:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ are continuous on $[a,b]$, and $\|u(s)\|\le M$, $\|v(s)\|\le N$ there, then $K(t-s)(u(s),v(s))$ is Bochner integrable from $a$ to $t$ for every $t\in[a,b]$, and its integral is continuous in $t$ on $[a,b]$. In addition, when $t-a\le1$, its norm is at most $4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$. Such finite $M,N$ exist by compactness of $[a,b]$. Integrability and continuity have no restriction on $b-a$. The interval of length zero is allowed, with integral zero. Values of the curves outside $[a,b]$ and the value of $K(0)$ do not affect the conclusion.
notes.Breakdown.WeakPeriodicSimilarityProfileE:
There exist $S>0$, an orthogonal map $R$, fields $W(s,y)$, $G(s,y)$ and $H(s,y)$ each admitting a measurable representative for space-time Lebesgue measure, and a finite real $C$, with the following properties. The velocity $W$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, and $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ at every point. For every $s$, $G(s,\cdot)$ is the distributional spatial derivative of $W(s,\cdot)$; for almost every $s$, $H(s,\cdot)$ is the distributional derivative of $G(s,\cdot)$. These distributional derivative conditions include local integrability. The velocity is divergence-free almost everywhere in space at every time. One constant bounds $\int|W(s)|^6\,dy$ and $\int\|G(s)\|^2\,dy$ for every $s$, and $\int_0^S\int\|H\|^2\,dy\,ds<\infty$. The norms of $G,H$ are operator norms; they differ by fixed dimension-dependent factors from the sums of squared coordinate derivatives used in the paper. For every smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free space-time test field $\varphi$, the integrand is integrable and
$\int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3}[-W\cdot\partial_s\varphi-W\cdot\varphi-\frac12W\cdot(y\cdot\nabla)\varphi+\sum_iG(e_i)\cdot\partial_i\varphi-\sum_iW_iW\cdot\partial_i\varphi],ds\,dy=0$.
Finally $W$ is not zero almost everywhere in space-time. The expression is the pressure-free weak similarity equation: the pressure term disappears because the test fields are divergence-free. No pressure, smoothness, pointwise decay, quantitative closeness to an approximate field, or prescribed value of $R$ is part of this conclusion. Nontriviality here means nonzero on a set of positive space-time measure, rather than merely at a single point.
notes.Breakdown.WeakProfile.constOfWeakDeriv_h: The formal distributional step identifies a weak time derivative by testing and controls its primitive up to constants. The paper gives the physical change of variables.
notes.Breakdown.WeakProfile.mildFromGood_holds: Here $X$ is the divergence-free homogeneous Sobolev space on $\mathbb R^3$, represented by its $L^6$ velocity, with $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$. The periodic forcing space is $\mathcal H_{\rm div}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3))$. Its elements, and the periodic perturbations, are identified when equal almost everywhere. Let $l<r$, let $y:(l,r)\to X$ be strongly measurable up to a null set and bounded in $X$, and let $E\subset(l,r)$ have full measure. Choose $t_0\in(l,r)$ and define $z(t)=e^{(t-t_0)\Delta}y(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^tB_{t-\tau}(y(\tau),y(\tau))\,d\tau$. Assume $z$ is continuous on $[t_0,r)$ and $z(t)=y(t)$ for every $t\in E$ with $t\geq t_0$, as well as the bilinear integrability statement for bounded measurable $X$-valued curves. Then, for every $t_0\leq a<b<r$, the formal statement proves that $z$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, that its Duhamel integral is integrable there, and that $z(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}z(a)+\int_a^tB_{t-\tau}(z(\tau),z(\tau))\,d\tau$ for every $t\in[a,b]$. The theorem concerns this constructed representative. Identification with the originally specified physical velocity at every time needs continuity of both representatives. It does not itself identify the spatial kernel of $B$.
notes.Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalCurve: Here $X$ is the divergence-free homogeneous Sobolev space on $\mathbb R^3$, represented by its $L^6$ velocity, with $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$. The periodic forcing space is $\mathcal H_{\rm div}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3))$. Its elements, and the periodic perturbations, are identified when equal almost everywhere. For any curve $x:\mathbb R\to X$ and any reference similarity time $s_0$, the definition gives $u(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}x(s_0-\log(1-t))$, where $(D_\mu v)(z)=\sqrt\mu\,v(\sqrt\mu z)$ for $\mu>0$. It is a function on all real $t$. For $t<1$, the scale and logarithm argument are positive and the formula has its ordinary physical meaning. For $t\geq1$, the dilation is set to zero for nonpositive scale; in particular real division by zero is assigned zero at $t=1$. Thus this total extension has no asserted physical interpretation at or after time one. To read the paper's formula take $s_0=0$ and $x(s)=\mathcal W(s/S)$. The definition alone proves no continuity, equation or norm bound.
notes.Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalIdentity_o:
Let $X=\dot H^1_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3)$, represented by its $L^6$ velocities and norm $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_2$. Fix $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and a curve $x:\mathbb R\to X$ that is strongly measurable up to a null set and satisfies $\|x(s)\|_X\le M$ for every $s$. The formal statement assumes the similarity weak identity tested against the scaled products of a compactly supported smooth time function and a compactly supported smooth solenoidal spatial field, together with the physical pairing and scaling identities for this Sobolev representation. Put $u(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}x(s_0-\log(1-t))$ for $t<1$, where $D_\mu v(z)=\mu^{1/2}v(\mu^{1/2}z)$ for $\mu>0$. The conclusion is the nonlinear weak evolution identity on $(-1,1)$:
$\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb R}\eta'(t)\int_{\mathbb R^3}u\cdot\psi\,dz\,dt=-\int_{\mathbb R}\eta(t)\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl[u\cdot\Delta\psi+(u\otimes u):\nabla\psi\bigr]\,dz\,dt,$
for $\eta\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))$ and $\psi=-\Delta\varphi$, with $\varphi\in C_{c,\rm div}^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$. Here the tensor contraction is $\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_i\psi_j$. The restricted spatial test family comes from the homogeneous $H^1$ inner product. The field has no assumed recurrence or periodicity. The nonlinear weak identity displayed in §7.10, immediately before (7.64), holds for every compactly supported smooth solenoidal spatial test and all compactly supported time tests in $(-\infty,1)$. The formal conclusion has the restricted test family and time interval stated above. The linked equation (7.41) has a different role: it is a linear change-of-variables identity for general locally integrable fields and contains no nonlinear term. The formal conclusion is used subsequently to obtain a mild evolution. Its definition extends $u$ by zero for $t\ge1$; no equation is asserted on that range.

Assume there is a dense set of $f\in\mathcal X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. For $0<T\le1$ and every continuous background $f:[0,T]\to\mathcal X$, the formal statement proves that $g\mapsto\int_0^TK(T-s)(f(s),g(s))\,ds$ is a compact operator from $C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ with its supremum norm to $\mathcal X$. Composing it with the bounded map from initial data to the linearized trajectory gives compactness of the correction to the free endpoint map. The conclusion does not assert compactness of the entire trajectory-valued Duhamel operator.

notes.Breakdown.extended_certificate_breakdown:
**Hypothesis.** The hypothesis is existence of certificate data in a finite parameter dimension satisfying the formal conditions corresponding to §§7.1–7.3. In mathematical terms the data consist of a dimension $n\ge0$, a parameter set $\mathcal K$ given by the coordinate intervals and the remaining weighted Euclidean ball in (7.29), periods $0<S(\alpha)\le S_{\max}$, approximate divergence-free unit-period fields $W^{\mathrm a}_\alpha$, a comparison field, finitely many forcing and constraint fields, the weight $0<w_*\le w(y)\le w^*$, and constants and adjoint fields for the residual, coercivity, smallness and parameter-enclosure inequalities. These are hypotheses for every parameter and, in the coercivity and adjoint estimates, every admissible perturbation; a numerical witness to them is not produced by this implication.

The formal input differs from the paper's definition in specific ways. The approximate field is $C^1$ jointly in all real parameter, time and space variables, including parameters outside $\mathcal K$, and is unit-periodic there. A supplied weak spatial Hessian must exist at every time and satisfy the additional uniform bound $C_{\mathrm a}(1+|y|)^{-3}$, in operator norm. The first derivative decay bound is also in operator norm; (7.8) uses the Frobenius norm, and conversion at a fixed constant costs at most $\sqrt3$. The weight is measurable, bounded above and below by positive finite constants, and invariant under the spatial isometries of the prescribed symmetries. The finite family representing the row norm is orthonormal, with nonnegative weights bounded by $c_0^2$; the paper instead uses pairwise orthogonal fields of norm at most $c_0$. Multiplying each orthonormal field by the square root of its weight gives the paper’s seminorm. The constraint matrix fields are only assumed measurable with a finite square integral on $[0,1]$; their periodicity is not a separate formal certificate hypothesis, and the time-circle construction uses the periodic extension of their restriction to $[0,1)$. The coefficient $c_2$ is explicitly nonnegative. Each adjoint field has a common spatial $L^2$ bound at every time, in addition to periodicity. The residual is a specified expression using a supplied measurable periodic vector field whose pairing with compact solenoidal tests vanishes. No scalar pressure is supplied by this hypothesis; the paper allows a residual specified only modulo gradients. The integer used in the supremum estimate may be $1$, or $2$ if a half-period symmetry is present; the paper's convention (7.6) chooses $2$ whenever such a symmetry is available. All coefficient and residual norms, positivity conditions and inequalities (7.18)–(7.37) are assumptions in the corresponding formal certificate, subject to these encodings. The index sets may be empty, and the parameter set need not have interior. The divisions by $S(\alpha)$, $w_*$, the positive forcing weight and the nonzero coordinate scales are legitimate under the stated positivity and nonvanishing assumptions.

**Conclusion.** For every viscosity $\nu>0$ there exists a smooth, compactly supported divergence-free datum $u_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ for which no pair $(u,p)$ has all of the following properties: it is smooth on $[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3$ up to the initial time, has $u(0)=u_0$, satisfies $\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=\nu\Delta u-\nabla p$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ at every $t>0$ and every spatial point, and has $\sup_{t\ge0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(t,x)|^2\,dx<\infty$. The formal functions are defined for all real times; smoothness and the equation are restricted to the nonnegative and positive time ranges just stated, so negative times carry no condition. The datum may depend on $\nu$. This conclusion does not name a finite blow-up time or give a blow-up rate, a limiting profile, or a chosen certificate parameter.

**Comparison with Corollary 7.2.** The corollary invokes the full conclusion of Theorem 1.1 for the profile of Theorem 7.1. The formal statement gives the nonexistence conclusion above, for every positive viscosity, and omits the constructed solution's finite time, rate and limiting profile. The paper normalizes viscosity to one; its scaling gives the same extension to other positive viscosities.

lean.name: Breakdown.TransferHolds
lean.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$ be a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau)$ be symmetric bounded bilinear maps, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0,\tau>0$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, where $C_K\ge0$. For $\mu>0$, assume strongly continuous dilations satisfying $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For every $f$ in a dense subset of $X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with these operators at all their defined real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $S>0$ and $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For every $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to converge and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. The application is $X=\dot H^1_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3)$ and $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$. For every dense real linear subspace $C\subset X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, the conclusion chooses a datum $u(0)\in C$ with $\|u(0)-w(0)\|<\varepsilon$ and a continuous mild curve on $[0,1)$. For some $A\in\mathbb R$ and $\kappa>0$, it satisfies $\|D_{1-t}u(t)-w(-\log(1-t))\|\le A(1-t)^\kappa$ for every $0\le t<1$. Here mildness means $u(t)=G(t)u(0)+\int_0^tK(t-r)(u(r),u(r))\,dr$, with each Bochner integral convergent. It does not assert smooth physical representatives or one kinetic-energy bound on the full lifespan, and it does not state the two-sided rate in Theorem 1.1.

lean.fidelity_note:
The formal statement defines an existence assertion on the unit torus. There are a smooth field $u_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with period one in each coordinate and zero divergence, a real $T>0$, and a continuous mild curve $u$ on $[0,T)$ whose initial state is the Fourier representation of $u_0$, such that $\sup_{0\le t<T}\|u(t)\|=\infty$. The periodic state has coordinates $\sqrt{1+4\pi^2|k|^2}\,\widehat u(k)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^3$, with conjugate symmetry and $k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0$; its norm is the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm on the unit cell. The zero coefficient is allowed, so this state space does not impose zero mean. The initial-field map returns zero outside its admissible Fourier class; smooth periodic solenoidal data belong to that class. Mild means the heat-plus-quadratic Bochner equation for every $0\le t<T$, with convergent time integrals. The assertion imposes neither $T\le1$ nor either estimate in (1.7), gives no local comparison on $B_{1/16}$, and states unboundedness rather than a specified limit or rate at $T$. It contains no smooth velocity-pressure representative of the curve. The formal statement is only this existence condition; a separate construction proves it from a profile.

For $\theta>0$, the substitutions $\chi_n=\theta^nx_n$ and $f_n=\theta^nc_n$ yield $\chi_{n+1}=M\chi_n+f_n$. The recurrence definition presupposes its sequence $c_n$ and defines none of those physical-to-period maps. It is a related discrete formulation only.

lean.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. On $Y=C([0,L];X)$ with its supremum norm, set $a_n(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-t))$, $A_nz(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(a_n(r),z(r))\,dr$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$, and $Ev=D_\mu v(L)$. lean.name: Breakdown.StepDataStatement
lean.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Suppose $G(t)$, $t\ge0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear family, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $\mu>0$, suppose the dilations are strongly continuous, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. For a dense linear subspace $C\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the formal assertion chooses $k\ge1$, $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $L=1-\mu\le t_0$ and $\mu^{1/4}<\theta<1$. On $Y=C([0,L];X)$ with its supremum norm, set $a_n(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-t))$, $A_nz(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(a_n(r),z(r))\,dr$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$, and $Ev=D_\mu v(L)$. It gives $\|A_n\|\le1/4$, a finite-dimensional $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C$, and a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$. Writing $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, the conclusions are $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. The physical datum correction is $Je\in J(V)$; its bound also uses $\|J\|$. The chosen short-interval weight satisfies $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Consequently $\Theta=\theta^k$ lies in $(e^{-S/4},1)$ and $\kappa=-(k/S)\log\theta$ lies in $(0,1/4)$. The paper names $\kappa$ and the whole-period weight explicitly; the formal assertion names $k$ and $\theta$ and does not introduce a global weighted curve norm.

Set $S_n=E(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$ and $M=\rho^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$, and assume $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, $P^2=P$, $PM=MP$, $PJ=P$. For $0\le r_1<\theta^k<r_2$, require $\|M^n(I-P)\|\le Kr_1^n$, $\|Px\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|M^nPx\|$ for all $n\ge0,x\in X$, and surjectivity of $M$ on $\operatorname{ran}P$. lean.name: Breakdown.orbitSeq
lean.fidelity_note: For a bounded linear operator $M$ on a real normed space, a real $\theta$, a prescribed source sequence $c_n$ and an initial value $x_0$, the formal definition is $x_{n+1}=\theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ for natural $n$. It has no boundedness or decay conclusion. At $\theta=0$ division is assigned zero; the dichotomy arguments impose $\theta>0$. For $\theta>0$, the substitutions $\chi_n=\theta^nx_n$ and $f_n=\theta^nc_n$ yield $\chi_{n+1}=M\chi_n+f_n$. The paper's (4.13) instead defines rescaled curves $v_n,g_n$ and derives its forcing $f_n$ from a global source. The recurrence definition presupposes its sequence $c_n$ and defines none of those physical-to-period maps. It is a related discrete formulation only.

lean.name: Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation
lean.fidelity_note: Let $X,E$ be real Banach spaces, $0<L\le1$, $0<\theta<1$, $c\in\mathbb R$, and $C_K\ge0$. Assume $a_n,r_n\in Y$, $\sup_n\|a_n\|_Y<\infty$, $a_n=\Gamma_na_n(0)+B_n(a_n,a_n)+r_n$, $\|r_n\|_Y\le\theta^n\rho$, and $a_{n+1}(0)=c\,a_n(L)$. lean.name: Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties_holds
lean.fidelity_note:
Let $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and satisfy $\partial_sW+\frac12W+\frac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ and $\nabla\cdot W=0$ for every $(s,y)$. Assume, uniformly in $s,y$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|_{\rm op}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the three integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. These assumptions imply $C\ge0$; recurrence and nonvanishing are not required here. The norm on a first derivative is its operator norm; the paper's pointwise matrix norm is the square root of the sum of the squared column lengths, which is at most $\sqrt3$ times this norm.

Put $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $\chi$ be the fixed smooth cutoff with $0\le\chi\le1$, equal to one for $|x-a|\le1/16$ and zero for $|x-a|\ge1/8$. For $T>0$, $t<T$, set $\ell=T-t$, $s=-\log(\ell/T)$ and $g(x)=\ell^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)$. Define $A_g(x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,g(a+\sigma(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\sigma$, $\bar u(x)=\chi(x)g(x)+\nabla\chi(x)\times A_g(x)$, and $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(a+\sqrt\ell\,y)$. Thus $f$ is the cutoff expressed in similarity coordinates; its inner and outer radii are $1/(16\sqrt\ell)$ and $1/(8\sqrt\ell)$. Put $x_a=a+(3/32)e_1$ and $\bar p(x)=\chi(x)\ell^{-1}[q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)-q(s,(x_a-a)/\sqrt\ell)]$.

For every $T>0$, the formal statement proves that $(t,x)\mapsto\bar u(t,x)$ is smooth on $(-\infty,T)\times\mathbb R^3$, is divergence-free, vanishes for $|x-a|\ge1/8$, and equals $g$ for $|x-a|\le1/16$. It also proves smoothness and the same outer support for $\bar p(t,x)=\chi(x)[\ell^{-1}q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)-\ell^{-1}q(s,(x_a-a)/\sqrt\ell)]$, where $x_a=a+(3/32)e_1$ is fixed. Thus each spatial cutoff is in $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$. The centre, radii, time interval and pressure normalization are fixed as stated; an arbitrary radius $r$ is absent from the assertion. All logarithms, square roots and quotients used for $t<T$, $T>0$ have their ordinary positive arguments. The result gives no quantitative norm estimate.

The formal theorem applies the solenoidal cutoff after scaling to the unit cell: it agrees with the centered self-similar field on radius $1/16$ and vanishes outside radius $1/8$, for all $t<T$. The paper states the corresponding radii $L/16,L/8$ on the large torus.

The rescaled cutoff is $f_{T,t}(y)=\sqrt h\,\bar u_T(t,a+\sqrt h\,y)$; its outer and inner radii are $r=1/(8\sqrt h)$ and $r/2$.

$\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb R^3}|\nabla(W(s,y)-f_{T,t}(y))|^2\,dy\le\varepsilon.$
The threshold may depend on the profile and $\varepsilon$, and is uniform in $T,t$. The conclusion is qualitative and contains no explicit power of $r$.

The periodic space is the real solenoidal $H^1$ space on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. The zero Fourier coefficient is allowed. The whole-space space $X$ consists of solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ with norm $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_2$.

Put $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$, and let $w(x)$ be coordinatewise reduction modulo $\mathbb Z^3$ to the unit cell centred at $a$. For $\mu>0$, define $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$. Assume $g\in C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $\operatorname{supp}g\subset\bar B_b$, $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$ and $\sqrt\mu\,b\le1/8$.

The formal statement asserts the exact identity
$\displaystyle \|\mu^{1/4}g_\mu\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}^2=\|\nabla g\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}^2+\mu\|g\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}^2.$
The Fourier representation of a physical field is assigned zero when its weighted coefficients do not belong to the solenoidal square-summable space; the smoothness, support and divergence assumptions ensure the intended representation here.

The formal squared periodic norm also contains the scaled squared $L^2$ norm. The equality in (6.5) uses the homogeneous norm on the large torus.

lean.name: Breakdown.Periodic.approxSizes
lean.fidelity_note:
The proof assumes five analytic properties, each for all inputs of the indicated class. For every smooth solenoidal field supported in $\bar B_b$ at an admissible scale $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, the field $\mu^{1/4}g_\mu$, with $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$, $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and coordinate reduction $w$ to the unit cell, has squared periodic norm $\|\nabla g\|_2^2+\mu\|g\|_2^2$. For every similarity profile with the smoothness, equation and decay bounds stated below, its cutoff velocity and the pressure $p^{\mathrm a}(t,x)=\chi(x)[p^*(t,x)-p^*(t,a+(3/32)e_1)]$, where $p^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1}q(\log(T/(T-t)),(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$, are smooth for $t<T$, supported in $\bar B_{1/8}(a)$, the velocity is solenoidal, and it agrees with the centered self-similar field on $\bar B_{1/16}(a)$. Its normalized interval curves have their defining formula and satisfy $a_{n+1}(0)=\lambda^{1/4}a_n(1-\lambda)$ for $0<T\le1$ and $0<\lambda<1$. Finally, for every smooth solenoidal field with $|g(x)|\le C/(1+|x|)$ and $\|Dg(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C/(1+|x|)^2$, its whole-space Fourier embedding is linear under addition, subtraction and real scalar multiplication and has squared norm $\int|\nabla g|^2$. These are the five extra premises of this proof theorem. Its conclusion is the uniform approximate-interval bound below.

Assume that $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ are smooth, that $\operatorname{div}W=0$, and that $\partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ for every $(s,y)$. A single constant $C$ bounds $\|D^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla q(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in $s$. The norms of $D^jW$ are multilinear operator norms; for $j=1$ the paper’s Frobenius norm is between the operator norm and $\sqrt3$ times that norm.

The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

For $T>0$ and $t<T$, put $s=\log(T/(T-t))$ and $u_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$, where $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. Choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi$, equal to one on $\bar B_{1/16}(a)$ and zero when $|x-a|\ge1/8$. Put $A_g(x)=\int_0^1\tau g(a+\tau(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\tau$. The cutoff is $\bar u_T=\chi u_T^*+\nabla\chi\times A_{u_T^*}$, which equals $\operatorname{curl}(\chi A_{u_T^*})$ when $u_T^*$ is solenoidal.

Write $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$, $t_n=T-\mu_n$, $\ell=1-\lambda$, and $a_n(s)=\mu_n^{1/4}u^{\mathrm a}(t_n+\mu_ns)$ for $0\le s\le\ell$, where $u^{\mathrm a}$ is the unit-periodic extension of the solenoidal cutoff of the centered self-similar field. The index $n$ is a nonnegative integer and the interval norm is the supremum norm.

Assume $0<\lambda<1$ and $c>0$ with $c\le\|W(s)\|_X$ for every real $s$.

The formal statement proves the existence of $T_0>0$ and $M\in\mathbb R$ such that, for every $0<T<T_0$ and every $n\ge0$, $\|a_n\|_{C([0,\ell];H^1)}\le M$ and $c/2\le\|a_n(s)\|_{H^1}$ for every $0\le s\le\ell$. Here $\|W(s)\|_X=\|\nabla W(s)\|_2$. The curve is represented by its continuous restriction; the general construction uses zero if continuity fails, while the profile hypotheses ensure continuity here. The statement gives no equality with a whole-space homogeneous norm and no explicit factor $c_*-CL^{-1/2}$.

The theorem derives positive upper and lower bounds for normalized approximate intervals from the transplant, cutoff, matching and embedding properties. It does not export the precise large-torus expression in (6.5).

The number $m$ is fixed. 

Use the whole-space heat flow, Navier–Stokes bilinear kernel and spatial dilation $D_\lambda f(x)=\lambda^{1/2}f(\lambda^{1/2}x)$, and assume the periodic kernel estimate $\|K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)\|\le C_{\mathbb T}\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Let $P>0$, let $k>0$ be an integer, put $\lambda=e^{-P/k}$ and $\ell=1-\lambda\le1/2$, and choose $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta<1$ and $b>0$. The preceding finite-sum approximation is taken on $[0,\ell]$. Let $E$ be finite dimensional, let $J:E\to X$ be bounded linear, and let $e\mapsto\psi_e$ be linear, with each $\psi_e$ smooth, compactly supported, solenoidal, supported in $\bar B_b$, and representing $Je$.

The three spaces used below are the bounded sequences of continuous $X$-valued, periodic-$H^1$-valued and local-data-valued curves on $[0,\ell]$. Each has norm $\sup_n\sup_{0\le s\le\ell}\|v_n(s)\|$. Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$, let $w$ reduce coordinates to the unit cell centered at $a$, and put $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$. The periodic datum map is $J_{\mathbb T}e=T^{1/4}(\psi_e)_T$, where $(\psi_e)_T(x)=T^{-1/2}\psi_e((w(x)-a)/\sqrt T)$.

Here are the operators whose differences the formal statement controls. Whole-space restriction $R$ records $1_{\bar B_b}\partial_jv_n$ and $1_{\bar B_b}v_n$. Periodic restriction $R_{\mathbb T}$ records $1_{\bar B_b}\mu_n^{3/4}\partial_jz_n(a+\sqrt{\mu_n}y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu_n^{1/4}z_n(a+\sqrt{\mu_n}y)$. The periodic restriction is zero if $0<\mu_n\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt{\mu_n}b\le1/8$ fail; sufficiently small $T$ ensures these conditions. For a local tuple $\zeta=(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ put $F_{\varphi,\zeta}=1_{\bar B_b}\sum_j(\varphi_jA_j+v_j\partial_j\varphi)$. The whole-space interaction is
$\displaystyle (B\zeta)_n(s)=-\sum_l\int_0^s\alpha_{n,l}(\sigma)e^{(s-\sigma)\Delta}\mathbb PF_{\varphi_{n,l},\zeta_n(\sigma)}\,d\sigma.$
For $B_{\mathbb T}$ replace the projected heat field under the integral by
$\displaystyle \mu_n^{-1/4}e^{\mu_n(s-\sigma)\Delta}\mathbb P\bigl[F_{\varphi_{n,l},\zeta_n(\sigma)}((w(x)-a)/\sqrt{\mu_n})\bigr].$
The minus sign and weights are unchanged. These definitions use the bounded integral operators supplied by the heat estimates; their general definitions assign zero if the required bounded realization does not exist.

The preceding-interval maps satisfy $(Sy)_0=(S_{\mathbb T}z)_0=0$ and, for $n\ge1$,
$\displaystyle (Sy)_n(s)=\theta^{-1}e^{s\Delta}D_\lambda y_{n-1}(\ell),\qquad (S_{\mathbb T}z)_n(s)=\frac{\lambda^{1/4}}\theta e^{\mu_ns\Delta}z_{n-1}(\ell).$
The datum maps have $(Ge)_0(s)=e^{s\Delta}Je$ and $(G_{\mathbb T}e)_0(s)=e^{Ts\Delta}J_{\mathbb T}e$, with all later entries zero. The propagation bounds are $\|S\|,\|S_{\mathbb T}\|\le\lambda^{1/4}/\theta<1$, so $I-S$ and $I-S_{\mathbb T}$ have ordinary bounded inverses. The general inverse convention assigns zero to a noninvertible operator, which is excluded here.

For every $\delta>0$, the formal statement asserts a $T_0>0$ such that, for every $0<T\le1$ with $T<T_0$, and the datum map just specified,
$\displaystyle \|R_{\mathbb T}(I-S_{\mathbb T})^{-1}B_{\mathbb T}-R(I-S)^{-1}B\|\le\delta,\qquad \|R_{\mathbb T}(I-S_{\mathbb T})^{-1}G_{\mathbb T}-R(I-S)^{-1}G\|\le\delta.$
The threshold is uniform in the sequence index. No explicit rate in $T$ or the paper’s large torus period is asserted.

The formal assertion makes the localized operators arbitrarily close for sufficiently small $T$, after summing preceding-interval propagation. It gives neither the explicit rate $L^{-2}$ nor this single integral-operator difference.

For a dense set of inputs $u$, each map $K(\tau)(u,\cdot)$ is compact when $\tau>0$. Put $\lambda=e^{-P/k}$ and $\ell=1-\lambda$, where $P$ is real and $k$ is a natural number. The definition itself permits degenerate parameters, uses zero for sequence operators that have no bounded realization, and takes division by zero to be zero. Those values are excluded by the stated application hypotheses. It does not isolate the cutoff error in (6.14).

Assume that $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ are smooth, that $\operatorname{div}W=0$, and that $\partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ for every $(s,y)$. The norms of $D^jW$ are multilinear operator norms; for $j=1$ the paper’s Frobenius norm is between the operator norm and $\sqrt3$ times that norm.

The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

For $T>0$ and $t<T$, put $s=\log(T/(T-t))$ and $u_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$, where $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. First, on every interval $[0,\ell]$, $\ell>0$, the bounded bilinear curve operator is the Duhamel integral, has norm at most $4C_K\ell^{1/4}$ if $\ell\le1$, and the free curve operator is $x\mapsto G(\cdot)x$ with norm at most one. Second, if continuous curves $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a\le b$, have bounds $M,N$, their Duhamel integrals from $a$ to $t$ are integrable and continuous for every $t\in[a,b]$, and their norms are at most $4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$ when $t-a\le1$. For any finite cell and tree data and any real vector $x$ of global unknowns, the formal statement proves $\langle Nx,x\rangle=\langle A_0x,x\rangle+\sum_Q\langle A_QX_Qx,X_Qx\rangle+2\sum_\Pi\langle C_\Pi X_\Pi x,X_\Pi x\rangle$. Complex cell and rectangle forms are read by taking the real part of the Hermitian quadratic expression. The total matrix is the sum of all attached forms after their embedding in the global coordinates; the two occurrences of each auxiliary matrix have opposite signs and cancel. No analytic condition on a perturbation, no positivity, and no node inequality is needed for this algebraic identity. The matrices passed between nodes are arbitrary and do not enter the total sum.

The complete formal condition includes these two comparisons and also the row-sum residual test, symmetry, positive weights and pivot lower bounds. At one node, let $A=N_\xi+\sum_{\xi'}V_{\xi'}$, with the sum over its children, and let $V_\xi$ be the matrix passed to its parent. Given pivots $\mathcal U_\xi$ and columns $Y_\xi$, the condition supplies symmetric $H,K$, symmetric entrywise nonnegative $H',K'$, positive weights $w_j$, real $p_j,m_j$, and a rectangular real matrix $Y'$. For every real $x$ it requires $\langle Hx,x\rangle\le\langle Ax,x\rangle+\langle H'|x|,|x|\rangle$ and $\langle V_\xi x,x\rangle\le\langle Kx,x\rangle-\sum_{j\notin\mathcal U_\xi}m_jx_j^2+\langle K'|x|,|x|\rangle$. For each row, $w_i\sum_j(|B_{ij}|+H'_{ij}+K'_{ij})/w_j\le m_i$, where $B=H-\operatorname{diag}_{\mathcal U_\xi}(p)-Y'Y'^T+Y_\xi Y_\xi^T-K$ and the diagonal is zero off the pivots. On each pivot $\underline p_{\xi,j}\le p_j-m_j$. Here $|x|$ means componentwise absolute value. All spaces are finite-dimensional and the forms are real. The positive weights exclude zero denominators. These are assumptions on the supplied node matrices and bounds; they perform no numerical verification themselves.
